Conversation Lab proposes fictional practice for first-time team leads. The supplied situation is specific: a handoff note was absent on Monday, the next shift repeated a check, and the lead has not heard the colleague’s account. These observations do not establish carelessness, a capability deficit, responsibility for the repeated check or a causal relationship between the missing note and that check.

The intended task is to construct and reconsider a conversation proposal: an observation, an invitation to hear the colleague’s account and a feasible next move. New leads, colleagues, managers, learning teams and employee representatives are prospective affected groups. None have participated in this rehearsal.

Sequence 2 explicitly preserves the parent framing, Map and Design as background. It also supplies a parent Design response to a hypothetical interruption on a shared workstation. That interruption was not observed. Sequence 5 develops the new situation board, authored dialogue, support dependencies and paper activity. Neither event establishes approval or effectiveness.

The Systems engineer challenge is that a dependency label can coexist with an unconditional promise. A plan saying “we will use the template” remains infeasible when the template is inaccessible and no authorized person has resolved that barrier. The design therefore needs explicit rules connecting action, support status, authority and proposal wording.

Rival explanations include changed schedules, inaccessible tools, unclear ownership, inadequate coverage and conflicting expectations. Conversation difficulty may be secondary to these conditions. The fictional reveal establishes that the rota changed, the template was inaccessible to the colleague and the expected owner was unclear; it does not establish a complete causal explanation.

## Human and system capability

Human requirements: participants need discretion to retain or revise an interpretation, challenge suggested wording, decline sharing and stop. Leads need to distinguish actions within their role from changes requiring another person’s authority. Managers need to inspect protected time, staffing, access and ownership before expecting a shared next step. Facilitators need covered time, accessible materials and a way to support disagreement without judging communication style. No such resources, authority arrangements or participation protections have been secured.

System requirements: represent fictional facts, possible explanations and unanswered questions separately. Keep the participant’s current proposal distinct from historical wording and unconfirmed replacements. Represent workflow support as unknown, unavailable or available within the fictional exercise; never treat that selection as verification of real conditions. Preserve unresolved authority and colleague agreement explicitly.

Use fictional inputs only. Exclude employee ranking, consequential HR advice, identifiable recordings, profiling, telemetry, persistent storage and network requests. Maintain only the volatile state needed for interaction in the current frame. Do not use storage APIs, downloads or session logs to support recovery. Refresh or closure loses work. These are proposed implementation constraints, not inspected behavior.

Unknown access conditions include language needs, reading demands, assistive technology, device availability, suitable space and coverage. Untimed keyboard operation and plain wording are intended qualities requiring verification and affected-person review.

## Experience and decisions

Begin with the three supplied facts and separate areas for possible explanations and missing context. Present a small set of openings with concrete wording, plus pass and stop. An explicitly authored dialogue preview may show a colleague providing context, disputing an interpretation or postponing discussion. Label it where displayed as an invented possibility, not a prediction about a person.

After the initial proposal, reveal the changed rota, inaccessible template and unclear expected owner. Keep the initial proposal visible as history in the before/after comparison. Invite the participant to retain or revise their interpretation and next move; retaining an earlier choice is permitted. Describe its remaining uncertainties without a score or preferred-answer indicator.

When a proposed move depends on workflow support, reveal only the relevant support choices. For example, choosing template use exposes access and ownership dependencies. If access is unavailable or authority is unclear, the current proposal must say that use remains conditional and offer requesting support, revising the action or pausing. Do not silently assign the repair or ownership to a colleague, manager or next shift. Even when fictional support is available, label the action as a proposal awaiting the other person’s account and agreement.

Support and participation are separate decisions. A participant can finish the exercise with an unresolved question, a support request or a decision to pause. Finishing has no implication for capability or readiness. At most two optional open-text fields belong on the main path: replacement wording and an unresolved question. Choices and concrete previews should produce a usable plan without text entry.

For a correction, display the exact proposed replacement and its dependency summary before Apply or Cancel. Cancel leaves the current plan unchanged. Apply changes the current plan while retaining the original proposal as clearly labelled history. If relevant support or scenario context changes while a replacement is pending, mark that preview as needing review and require a new explicit Apply; do not silently apply stale wording.

Provide a continuously available Cover control. Cover removes the situation, history, current plan, optional text and pending preview from visual and ordinary assistive-technology access, and moves focus to a neutral screen. Resume is explicit. It restores the corrected current state and any still-valid pending review; rejected wording must not return as the current proposal. An optional orientation can show the current plan and unresolved support without demanding recall.

Provide a distinct Finish and clear for device handoff action. Review its effect, then require confirmation. Cancelling preserves the session. Confirming removes initial and current plans, optional text, pending replacements, support selections, dialogue state and second-situation progress. Return to a neutral start state without a recoverable summary. Clearing must also work from the covered screen without exposing the material being cleared.

Offer the optional second fictional situation from sequence 5: two shifts each understood the other to own the final checklist check. Use fewer initial suggestions, with optional support available on request. This is another supported practice opportunity, not evidence of transfer.

## Requirements and rationale

SE1 — Systems engineer origin, extending Workforce requirement R2 in sequence 5 and the context boundaries in sequence 2: bind proposed action wording to support and authority status. Selecting template use must expose access and ownership conditions; unavailable or unknown support must remain in the synthesis. Human reason: a lead cannot promise a repair outside their authority. System reason: descriptive dependency labels alone do not constrain an inconsistent plan. Acceptance check: with template access unavailable and owner unclear, the plan contains an unresolved support request or conditional next move and never asserts an agreed owner or unconditional template use. Whether these choices match real workflows remains unknown.

SE2 — Systems engineer origin, extending Workforce R1 and R3 in sequence 5: preserve contested interpretation and reciprocal agreement separately from fictional facts. The reveal must add context without replacing uncertainty with a diagnosis. Human reason: colleagues retain a perspective and a right to disagree. System reason: authored dialogue can otherwise appear to resolve the account automatically. Acceptance check: after the reveal, a participant can retain an interpretation, mark the account unresolved, choose postponement and produce a plan without a correctness judgment. The usefulness and acceptability of the wording remain unreviewed.

SE3 — Systems engineer origin, extending Workforce R4 in sequence 5 and the hypothetical interruption preserved by sequence 2: define correction, cover/resume and clearing as separate operations. Human reason: interruption should not erase work unexpectedly or expose reflection during a device handoff. System reason: historical, current and pending text can diverge and leak through incomplete resets. Acceptance check: Cancel preserves the current plan; Cover conceals every content surface and relocates focus; Resume restores current corrections; confirmed clearing resets all session content. No checks have occurred.

SE4 — Systems engineer origin, extending Workforce R5 in sequence 5: provide equivalent non-AI decisions and recovery materials. Human reason: device access, digital practice or retained reflection may be unacceptable. System reason: an alternative must carry the task rather than merely instruct people to discuss it. Acceptance check: a facilitator can run the initial situation, reveal, revision, dependency decision and optional second situation entirely from the materials below. Facilitation burden and accessibility remain pending review.

## Tradeoffs and alternatives

Support detail improves feasibility but can turn a short activity into an administrative exercise. Reveal details when the chosen next move depends on them; leave unresolved questions visible in the final plan. Authored choices reduce writing burden but constrain expression. Permit replacement wording, disagreement and stopping without rewarding script conformity.

Retain dissent that practice is the wrong intervention. A non-learning route is to clarify the current owner, repair template access, inspect the rota and arrange coverage before offering optional rehearsal. The candidate can expose these options but cannot authorize or verify organizational change.

Complete non-AI activity materials: a situation card with the three supplied facts; a board labelled Observed facts, Possible explanations and Missing context; opening cards reading “I noticed Monday’s handoff note was absent. What was happening from your perspective?”, “Can we check how the handoff was meant to work on Monday?” and “I need more context before deciding our next step”; blank replacement, Pass and Stop cards; and a reveal card reading “The rota changed. The template was inaccessible to the colleague. The expected owner was unclear. This is invented context, not a complete causal account.”

Provide two plan sheets labelled Initial proposal and Current proposal. Each has spaces for observation, invitation, proposed next move, needed workflow support, authority still needed and unresolved questions. Provide support cards for unknown, unavailable and available in this fictional situation, and a reminder that colleague agreement is unresolved. Include a blank cover sheet and the optional second-situation card: “Two shifts each understood the other to own the final checklist check.”

Facilitation instructions: establish voluntary participation, covered time, suitable space and participant-controlled disposal before starting. Do not solicit personal accounts. Invite an opening or written selection, release the reveal, and invite retaining or revising the plan. Pair the next move with support and authority; leave disagreement visible. A partner may dispute an assumption or postpone the discussion, without role-play being required. Offer the second situation with fewer suggestions or end. Cover sheets support interruption; resume only by participant choice. Do not collect, photograph or grade sheets. Participants may clear or dispose of their materials at the end under the agreed arrangement.

## Acceptance checks

Prepare a fictional interaction walkthrough: choose template use, set access unavailable and authority unclear, inspect the conditional proposal, then retain the initial interpretation while leaving the colleague’s account unanswered. Change a relevant support condition during a pending replacement; inspect whether renewed review is required. These checks address implementation behavior, not whether the participant learned.

Prepare a recovery walkthrough: enter fictional optional wording, apply a correction, open another replacement and cancel it, then cover using the keyboard. Inspect concealed content through ordinary accessibility navigation and focus position. Resume and inspect the corrected plan. Cancel clearing once, then confirm clearing from the covered screen; inspect that both situations and all draft states are reset. No results are available.

Inspect responsive readability, focus visibility, control labels, fictional labels and authored-dialogue boundaries. Inspect code and runtime behavior for network requests, storage and telemetry. A successful technical check would establish only the behavior checked. Human interaction review must separately examine comprehension, access, credible stopping and recovery burden.

## Evidence and unknowns

Actual earlier references are sequence 2, the preserved-parent verification event, and sequence 5, the Workforce specialist Design draft. The interruption within the parent material is hypothetical. The seed supplies the fictional source story and constraints. There is no participant observation, approved requirement, technical check result, field pilot or evidence of learning, transfer or flourishing.

What changes in this draft: sequence 5’s dependency display becomes an explicit rule for proposal wording; its recovery controls gain complete state coverage; and pending corrections require renewed review after relevant context changes. These refine the current Design artifact. They do not invalidate the preserved Map and do not require reopening it.

Unknowns include whether the task addresses an important lead need, whether participants understand conditional proposals, whether support decisions add excessive workload and whether organizational action is feasible. Later apparent improvement could reflect facilitator cues, familiarity, participant selection or repaired workflow. None can be attributed to practice without further evidence.

## Next decision

Carry these proposed requirements into the Design synthesis and then implement a candidate for fictional interaction review. This expert draft draws on sequences 6, 8 and 13. It is a rehearsal contribution, not an approved requirement. No participant observations, human approval, stakeholder consensus or measured learning outcomes exist. The review gate identified in sequence 8 remains unmet. This desk model supports review only; field evidence remains pending.

Challenge to the current model
Sequence 13 usefully models dependencies, participation states and recovery. Add an explicit account of what a learner might notice, decide and revise. Otherwise, completed practice could become the main visible signal despite the evidence limits in sequence 8. Activity completion, learning within practice, workplace adaptation and reciprocal usefulness are distinct claims. No transition between them should occur automatically.

Provisional learning model
Use a fictional situation as the unit of analysis. Record the situation’s ambiguity; the lead’s provisional interpretation; what the colleague can question or correct; candidate decisions; workplace dependencies; and evidence that could distinguish competing explanations. Keep these entries separate from private reflection and do not attach them to named employees.

A candidate practice cycle is: choose a fictional situation and format; identify an assumption; try an approach; receive descriptive feedback against participant-reviewed criteria; decide whether to revise; optionally try again with one changed condition. Prompts and examples may be reduced at the participant’s choice. This cycle is a design hypothesis, not evidence that learning or transfer will occur. Participants may pause, reject feedback or leave a disagreement unresolved.

Illustrative model entry
Situation: a fictional lead believes a missed handoff reflects carelessness. Candidate learning need: distinguish an observation from an interpretation and invite information that could change it. Colleague contribution: explain an unclear handoff expectation or challenge the concern. Context hypotheses: conflicting priorities, inadequate coverage or unclear responsibilities. Candidate responses include clarifying workflow, arranging support or practicing an opening question. Training is not selected until staffing and workflow explanations have been examined.

For a later fictional variation, change the authority boundary or introduce a conflicting account. Explore whether the participant recognizes the changed condition and explains a different choice. Repeating a memorized opening would answer a different question. Neither response establishes workplace readiness.

Feedback and dissent
Candidate feedback concerns are whether interpretations remain open to correction, whether both perspectives are considered and whether a proposed next step addresses the stated situation and constraints. Affected people must review these criteria before use. Do not reward speed, eye contact, confidence, script fidelity or agreement with the facilitator. A respectful conversation may end with unresolved disagreement. Preserve dissent over these criteria and over whether a capability map should exist at all.

Human requirements proposed for review
Affected people and representatives define acceptable reciprocal outcomes and disclosure boundaries. Facilitators negotiate feedback focus, distinguish learning difficulties from access or language demands and support correction without demanding conformity. Managers examine staffing, authority and workflow causes before prescribing training and arrange covered time. No owners, resources or participation protections have been secured.

System requirements proposed for review
Represent learning hypotheses, context hypotheses, disputed interpretations and absent evidence separately. Provide untimed accessible choices, optional prompts, pause, scenario replacement and editable reflection. Do not collect identifiable conversation recordings, rank employees or generate consequential scores. Attendance, refusal, format choice and missing evidence cannot establish capability. Sharing remains voluntary and separate from access to practice, with audience, retention and withdrawal limits reviewed by humans.

Evidence and next action
Proposed checks ask whether a fictional variation prompts reconsideration, whether feedback supports a participant-chosen revision and whether context barriers remain visible. These checks have not occurred. Later voluntary accounts of workplace use could inform adaptation hypotheses, but self-report alone cannot establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Consider familiarity, facilitator cues, selective participation and changed working conditions as rival explanations.

Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional scenarios, accessible written alternatives and private reflection as the non-AI option. Next, integrate this learning model into sequence 13’s dependency model and review it using fictional disagreement and workflow cases. It is a rehearsal contribution, not an approved requirement. No participant observations, stakeholder consensus, human authorization or measured learning outcomes exist. Field evidence remains pending.

Learning problem to investigate
The proposed capability map should distinguish knowing a conversation approach, using it in fictional practice, adapting it under workplace constraints and achieving an outcome that both people regard as respectful and useful. These are different claims. Course completion establishes neither readiness nor transfer. A polished rehearsal alone cannot establish workplace effectiveness, and a difficult workplace outcome does not by itself establish a capability deficit.

Discovery should explore three questions through fictional or generalized situations: What does the lead need to notice and decide? What should the colleague be able to question, clarify or change? What conditions make a useful conversation possible? Invite voluntary perspectives from leads, colleagues, managers, learning teams and employee representatives using the accessible choices proposed in sequence 6. Do not solicit recordings or identifiable accounts. Preserve conflicting answers rather than turning them into a common standard prematurely.

Provisional mapping template
For each fictional situation, record: the intended benefit for both people; decisions and adaptations that might require practice; competing workplace explanations; access and coverage conditions; unresolved dissent; and evidence needed to distinguish the hypotheses. Keep entries about situations and supports, not named employees.

Example hypothesis: a lead struggles to open a conversation when the concern is ambiguous. A possible learning need is distinguishing observations from interpretations and inviting correction. Rival explanations include unclear expectations, insufficient time to check the concern or fear of contradicting a manager. A next discovery step is to ask whether a fictional example presents a learning difficulty, a workplace barrier or both. No response or result is assumed.

Candidate learning approach
If discovery supports a learning need, consider short, protected practice sessions with participant-chosen fictional scenarios. Candidate supports include an optional example, prompts that can be reduced as desired, another attempt after feedback and a later variation requiring adaptation. These are design hypotheses to review, not a validated prescription. Participants should be able to pause, choose a written format, reject a scenario and challenge feedback. Agree what feedback concerns before practice; do not equate speed, eye contact, confidence or script fidelity with competence.

Evidence boundaries
A later evidence plan should distinguish participant experience, behavior in fictional practice and voluntary accounts of workplace use. Each answers a different question. Self-reported use may inform improvement but cannot alone establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Consider rival explanations such as changed workload, stronger managerial support, selective participation or familiarity with the practice task. Missing evidence must remain unknown, never a deficit. Evidence-sharing choices should be separate from access to learning, with audiences, retention and withdrawal limits established through human review.

Human and system responsibilities
Humans must judge acceptable outcomes, participation conditions, facilitation quality and whether staffing or workflow changes should precede training. Any system should support accessible practice and private reflection while keeping hypotheses, barriers and uncertainty visible. It cannot certify freely chosen participation or determine readiness from activity traces.

Non-AI option and next action

response.artifact_body:
## Problem and people

Conversation Lab proposes fictional practice for first-time team leads. The supplied story states that a handoff note was absent on Monday, the next shift repeated a check, and the lead has not heard the colleague’s account. The intended task is to distinguish observations from explanations, choose an opening, reconsider after additional context and construct a feasible conversation proposal. The absent note does not establish carelessness, responsibility or the cause of the repeated check.

New leads, colleagues, managers, learning teams and employee representatives are prospective affected groups. None have participated. This Human-centered designer contribution is an expert draft for Design synthesis, not an approved requirement.

Sequence 2 explicitly preserves the parent framing, Map and Design as background. Its parent Design includes a hypothetical interruption: a lead is recalled to cover a staffing gap while tentative practice wording remains visible on a shared workstation. No such incident was observed. Sequences 5 and 7 carry this concern into cover/resume, correction and complete clearing requirements.

The discipline-specific challenge is that technical correction and feasible dependencies are insufficient if the experience still centers the lead’s interpretation, treats suggested wording as obligatory or allocates organizational repair to the colleague. The interface must expose whose account is missing, whose agreement remains absent and who would bear proposed work.

## Human and system capability

Human requirements: participants need discretion to choose a written route, decline an example, pass, stop or leave disagreement unresolved without explaining why. Leads need to recognize the boundary between proposing an action and obtaining another person’s agreement. Managers must inspect protected time, staffing, suitable space, accessible workflow materials and authority before expecting participation or repair. Facilitators need time and support to accommodate different access needs without judging speed, speech, confidence or script conformity.

System requirements: provide a usable plan through choices and concrete previews without mandatory text entry. Keep fictional observations, possible explanations, missing accounts and unaccepted proposals distinct. Show relevant support and authority alongside the next move. Do not infer consent, capability, readiness or a colleague’s likely response from a selection.

The candidate must use fictional inputs only and exclude employee ranking, consequential HR advice, identifiable recordings, profiling, telemetry, storage and network requests. Recovery is confined to the current volatile session; refresh or closure loses work. No implementation has been inspected.

Language preferences, literacy demands, device availability, assistive technology, time, suitable space and participation protections are unknown. Plain wording, responsive layout and keyboard support are intended qualities requiring technical inspection and affected-person review. They do not establish accessibility for everyone.

## Experience and decisions

Open with a short situation board in a consistent reading order: Observed fictional facts, Possible explanations, Missing context. Do not require dragging cards, recognizing color or hovering. Explanation cards remain visibly tentative; selecting one does not move it into the facts area. Keep the colleague’s unheard account visible throughout.

Offer three concrete openings: an observation with an invitation, a question about the handoff process, and a decision to pause while checking context. Pass, Stop and Paper activity remain available without a justification field. Explain before entry that nothing is scored or shared and that work disappears on refresh or closure. Put detailed review information in Help.

Choosing an opening displays exact wording and explicitly authored possible dialogue. Include possibilities in which the colleague explains context, questions the interpretation or asks to discuss it later. These are invented examples, not predicted reactions. The participant can choose another opening, reject the example or continue with the account unresolved. No branch is marked as the correct response.

Reveal the supplied additional fictional context: the rota changed, the template was inaccessible to the colleague and the expected owner was unclear. Retaining or revising the initial interpretation are both legitimate. Describe which uncertainties and dependencies remain; do not praise revision itself or treat the reveal as a complete diagnosis.

Build a proposal comprising an observation, an invitation and a next move. When the participant chooses template use, reveal access and ownership conditions. If support is unknown or unavailable, offer requesting support, choosing another move or pausing. Display who would need to authorize a change and which work remains unassigned. Do not make the colleague responsible for fixing the inaccessible template by default. Even fictional support marked available leaves colleague agreement unresolved.

Show an Initial proposal and a Current proposal with an explicit statement of what changed or that the participant retained the original. Keep unresolved questions and support visible. A comparison need not appear simultaneously on a narrow screen; each version must remain clearly labelled and accessible without relying on visual position.

At most two optional open-text fields belong on the main path: replacement wording and an unresolved question. Choices must produce a concrete output when both are blank. Correction opens a review showing the exact replacement and dependency summary, followed by Apply and Cancel. Cancel preserves current wording and support state. If context changes during review, require renewed review before applying, as proposed in sequence 7. Authored suggestions must remain distinguishable from participant wording.

Cover immediately conceals all scenario, plan, optional text and pending-review content from visual and ordinary assistive-technology access, then places focus on a neutral screen. Resume is explicit and restores the current corrected state without demanding recall or an explanation. Finish and clear is separate: describe that all current-session material will be removed, require confirmation, and allow cancellation. Clearing must be possible from the covered screen without exposing its contents. Concealment does not establish shared-device suitability or prevent prior viewing.

Offer the optional second fictional situation with fewer suggestions: two shifts each understood the other to own the final checklist check. Keep support available on request and permit stopping. This is supported practice, not a test or evidence of transfer.

## Requirements and rationale

HCD1 — Human-centered designer origin, extending Workforce R1 in sequence 5 and Systems SE2 in sequence 7: make the situation board usable in a linear reading order, with text labels for facts, explanations and missing context. Human reason: device, vision, motor and reading conditions must not determine who can examine ambiguity. System reason: spatial layout and color alone cannot carry meaning. Acceptance check: a reviewer using only the keyboard can inspect every category, choose an explanation and still identify it as tentative; the colleague’s account remains missing after the reveal. Supplied context is the seed’s situation board; actual access needs remain unknown.

HCD2 — Human-centered designer origin, extending Workforce R3 in sequence 5 and Systems SE2 in sequence 7: make dissent and withholding agreement visible states rather than optional prose. Provide rejection of suggested wording, postponement and an unresolved-account route. Human reason: colleagues and leads retain different perspectives and participation choices. System reason: a selected dialogue branch must not appear to settle a conversation. Acceptance check: a reviewer can reject all examples and finish with an inquiry or pause, with no agreement or capability judgment in the output. Credible workplace refusal requires affected-person review.

HCD3 — Human-centered designer origin, extending Workforce R2 in sequence 5 and Systems SE1 in sequence 7: show responsibility and unassigned work beside each support-dependent next move. Human reason: an access barrier should not automatically create repair work for the colleague. System reason: conditional wording can still conceal workload allocation. Acceptance check: selecting inaccessible template and unclear owner produces a support request or pause, displays unresolved authority and does not assign repair to anyone. Actual support owners, resources and authority are unknown.

HCD4 — Human-centered designer origin, extending the hypothetical interruption preserved in sequence 2, Workforce R4 in sequence 5 and Systems SE3 in sequence 7: make recovery understandable and independent of recall. Use a persistent Cover control, a neutral covered screen, explicit Resume and separately confirmed clearing. Human reason: interruption and staffing demands should not require a participant to reconstruct or expose tentative reflection. System reason: historical, current and pending content need complete concealment and reset coverage. Acceptance check: apply a correction, cancel another, cover by keyboard and resume; current wording remains correct and concealed content is unavailable through ordinary accessibility navigation. Confirmed clearing removes both situations and all drafts. No check has occurred.

HCD5 — Human-centered designer origin, extending Workforce R5 in sequence 5 and Systems SE4 in sequence 7: provide equivalent written and facilitated paper decisions with low entry burden. Human reason: speech, role-play, devices and extensive writing may be unsuitable. System reason: an alternative must complete the same task without the candidate. Acceptance check: a reviewer can complete the digital route with no text entry and run the paper route using the materials below, including disagreement, revision and support decisions. Language suitability and facilitation workload remain pending review.

## Tradeoffs and alternatives

Choices reduce entry work but constrain expression; optional replacement wording and unresolved disagreement provide correction without requiring an essay. Examples offer support but can become scripts; rejection must not trigger corrective feedback. Before/after comparison makes revision inspectable but may privilege change; retaining a proposal must receive the same neutral treatment.

Retain dissent that conversation practice is the wrong response when access, staffing or ownership are unresolved. A non-learning option is to clarify the workflow, repair template access and arrange coverage before offering voluntary practice. The candidate cannot authorize or verify these changes.

Complete non-AI materials: a situation card reading, “A handoff note was absent on Monday. The next shift repeated a check. The new lead has not heard the colleague’s account”; a board labelled Observed facts, Possible explanations and Missing context; and opening cards reading, “I noticed Monday’s handoff note was absent. What was happening from your perspective?”, “Can we check how the handoff was meant to work on Monday?” and “I need more context before deciding our next step.” Include blank replacement, Pass and Stop cards.

Provide a reveal card reading, “The rota changed. The template was inaccessible to the colleague. The expected owner was unclear. This is invented context, not a complete explanation.” Provide response cards reading, “Here is additional context”, “I question that interpretation” and “I would prefer to discuss this later”. These support written selection; speech and role-play are optional.

Provide Initial proposal and Current proposal sheets with spaces for observation, invitation, next move, needed support, authority, work still unassigned and unresolved disagreement. Add support cards labelled Unknown, Unavailable and Available in this fictional situation. Provide a blank cover sheet and an optional second-situation card reading, “Two shifts each understood the other to own the final checklist check.”

Facilitator instructions: first arrange voluntary participation, covered time, accessible materials, suitable space and participant-controlled disposal. Present the situation and invite an opening or Pass. Release the reveal, then invite retaining or revising the proposal. Pair the next move with support, authority and workload; leave disagreement visible. Offer the second situation with fewer suggestions or end. Do not solicit personal accounts, collect or photograph sheets, grade wording or require sharing. Use the cover sheet for interruption and resume only by participant choice. Dispose of materials under the arrangement agreed before starting. These conditions have not been secured.

## Acceptance checks

Prepare a fictional agency walkthrough: choose an opening, reject the dialogue example, reveal context, retain an interpretation and finish with a support request while the colleague’s account and agreement remain unresolved. Inspect that no correctness label, completion penalty or readiness claim appears.

Prepare an access and recovery walkthrough: complete the main task without text entry using only the keyboard, inspect a narrow layout and meaningful labels, review and cancel a correction, then cover and resume. Inspect concealed content and focus through ordinary accessibility navigation. Cancel clearing once, then confirm it from the covered screen and inspect the complete reset. These are proposed checks, not results.

Practitioner and affected-person review should examine comprehension, dignity, language, credible passing, task burden and responsibility allocation. Technical inspection should separately examine storage, network behavior, focus and state handling. Passing technical checks would establish only the behavior inspected; learning, transfer, belonging and sustainable workload remain untested.

## Evidence and unknowns

Actual references are sequence 2, the preserved-parent verification event; sequence 5, the Workforce specialist draft; and sequence 7, the Systems engineer draft. The shared-workstation interruption in sequence 2 is hypothetical. The seed supplies invented source material and constraints. No new participant observation, authorization, consensus or measured outcome exists. Field evidence remains pending.

The design change after the preserved interruption is to make recovery participant-controlled, correction-aware and usable without recall, with confirmed clearing separate from concealment. This draft additionally makes dissent a concrete interaction and exposes workload allocation. These refine current Design; no supplied evidence invalidates the earlier Map.

Unknowns include whether the task reflects an important need, whether the choices represent affected people adequately and whether protected time and accessible support are feasible. Rival explanations for later apparent benefit include facilitator cues, familiarity, selective participation, repaired workflow and stronger managerial support. Revision, completion and second-situation performance cannot establish learning or transfer.

## Next decision

Incorporate these proposed interactions and acceptance cases into the Design synthesis and subsequent candidate Build. Keep practitioner and affected-person review of reciprocal agency, access, participation and workload pending. A future candidate is for human interaction and technical review; no field use, approval or efficacy decision is supported.

Conversation Lab proposes fictional practice for first-time team leads. The supplied situation is specific: a handoff note was absent on Monday, the next shift repeated a check, and the lead has not heard the colleague’s account. These observations do not establish carelessness, a capability deficit, responsibility for the repeated check or a causal relationship between the missing note and that check.

The intended task is to construct and reconsider a conversation proposal: an observation, an invitation to hear the colleague’s account and a feasible next move. New leads, colleagues, managers, learning teams and employee representatives are prospective affected groups. None have participated in this rehearsal.

Sequence 2 explicitly preserves the parent framing, Map and Design as background. It also supplies a parent Design response to a hypothetical interruption on a shared workstation. That interruption was not observed. Sequence 5 develops the new situation board, authored dialogue, support dependencies and paper activity. Neither event establishes approval or effectiveness.

The Systems engineer challenge is that a dependency label can coexist with an unconditional promise. A plan saying “we will use the template” remains infeasible when the template is inaccessible and no authorized person has resolved that barrier. The design therefore needs explicit rules connecting action, support status, authority and proposal wording.

Rival explanations include changed schedules, inaccessible tools, unclear ownership, inadequate coverage and conflicting expectations. Conversation difficulty may be secondary to these conditions. The fictional reveal establishes that the rota changed, the template was inaccessible to the colleague and the expected owner was unclear; it does not establish a complete causal explanation.

## Human and system capability

Human requirements: participants need discretion to retain or revise an interpretation, challenge suggested wording, decline sharing and stop. Leads need to distinguish actions within their role from changes requiring another person’s authority. Managers need to inspect protected time, staffing, access and ownership before expecting a shared next step. Facilitators need covered time, accessible materials and a way to support disagreement without judging communication style. No such resources, authority arrangements or participation protections have been secured.

System requirements: represent fictional facts, possible explanations and unanswered questions separately. Keep the participant’s current proposal distinct from historical wording and unconfirmed replacements. Represent workflow support as unknown, unavailable or available within the fictional exercise; never treat that selection as verification of real conditions. Preserve unresolved authority and colleague agreement explicitly.

Use fictional inputs only. Exclude employee ranking, consequential HR advice, identifiable recordings, profiling, telemetry, persistent storage and network requests. Maintain only the volatile state needed for interaction in the current frame. Do not use storage APIs, downloads or session logs to support recovery. Refresh or closure loses work. These are proposed implementation constraints, not inspected behavior.

Unknown access conditions include language needs, reading demands, assistive technology, device availability, suitable space and coverage. Untimed keyboard operation and plain wording are intended qualities requiring verification and affected-person review.

## Experience and decisions

Begin with the three supplied facts and separate areas for possible explanations and missing context. Present a small set of openings with concrete wording, plus pass and stop. An explicitly authored dialogue preview may show a colleague providing context, disputing an interpretation or postponing discussion. Label it where displayed as an invented possibility, not a prediction about a person.

After the initial proposal, reveal the changed rota, inaccessible template and unclear expected owner. Keep the initial proposal visible as history in the before/after comparison. Invite the participant to retain or revise their interpretation and next move; retaining an earlier choice is permitted. Describe its remaining uncertainties without a score or preferred-answer indicator.

When a proposed move depends on workflow support, reveal only the relevant support choices. For example, choosing template use exposes access and ownership dependencies. If access is unavailable or authority is unclear, the current proposal must say that use remains conditional and offer requesting support, revising the action or pausing. Do not silently assign the repair or ownership to a colleague, manager or next shift. Even when fictional support is available, label the action as a proposal awaiting the other person’s account and agreement.

Support and participation are separate decisions. A participant can finish the exercise with an unresolved question, a support request or a decision to pause. Finishing has no implication for capability or readiness. At most two optional open-text fields belong on the main path: replacement wording and an unresolved question. Choices and concrete previews should produce a usable plan without text entry.

For a correction, display the exact proposed replacement and its dependency summary before Apply or Cancel. Cancel leaves the current plan unchanged. Apply changes the current plan while retaining the original proposal as clearly labelled history. If relevant support or scenario context changes while a replacement is pending, mark that preview as needing review and require a new explicit Apply; do not silently apply stale wording.

Provide a continuously available Cover control. Cover removes the situation, history, current plan, optional text and pending preview from visual and ordinary assistive-technology access, and moves focus to a neutral screen. Resume is explicit. It restores the corrected current state and any still-valid pending review; rejected wording must not return as the current proposal. An optional orientation can show the current plan and unresolved support without demanding recall.

Provide a distinct Finish and clear for device handoff action. Review its effect, then require confirmation. Cancelling preserves the session. Confirming removes initial and current plans, optional text, pending replacements, support selections, dialogue state and second-situation progress. Return to a neutral start state without a recoverable summary. Clearing must also work from the covered screen without exposing the material being cleared.

Offer the optional second fictional situation from sequence 5: two shifts each understood the other to own the final checklist check. Use fewer initial suggestions, with optional support available on request. This is another supported practice opportunity, not evidence of transfer.

## Requirements and rationale

SE1 — Systems engineer origin, extending Workforce requirement R2 in sequence 5 and the context boundaries in sequence 2: bind proposed action wording to support and authority status. Selecting template use must expose access and ownership conditions; unavailable or unknown support must remain in the synthesis. Human reason: a lead cannot promise a repair outside their authority. System reason: descriptive dependency labels alone do not constrain an inconsistent plan. Acceptance check: with template access unavailable and owner unclear, the plan contains an unresolved support request or conditional next move and never asserts an agreed owner or unconditional template use. Whether these choices match real workflows remains unknown.

SE2 — Systems engineer origin, extending Workforce R1 and R3 in sequence 5: preserve contested interpretation and reciprocal agreement separately from fictional facts. The reveal must add context without replacing uncertainty with a diagnosis. Human reason: colleagues retain a perspective and a right to disagree. System reason: authored dialogue can otherwise appear to resolve the account automatically. Acceptance check: after the reveal, a participant can retain an interpretation, mark the account unresolved, choose postponement and produce a plan without a correctness judgment. The usefulness and acceptability of the wording remain unreviewed.

SE3 — Systems engineer origin, extending Workforce R4 in sequence 5 and the hypothetical interruption preserved by sequence 2: define correction, cover/resume and clearing as separate operations. Human reason: interruption should not erase work unexpectedly or expose reflection during a device handoff. System reason: historical, current and pending text can diverge and leak through incomplete resets. Acceptance check: Cancel preserves the current plan; Cover conceals every content surface and relocates focus; Resume restores current corrections; confirmed clearing resets all session content. No checks have occurred.

SE4 — Systems engineer origin, extending Workforce R5 in sequence 5: provide equivalent non-AI decisions and recovery materials. Human reason: device access, digital practice or retained reflection may be unacceptable. System reason: an alternative must carry the task rather than merely instruct people to discuss it. Acceptance check: a facilitator can run the initial situation, reveal, revision, dependency decision and optional second situation entirely from the materials below. Facilitation burden and accessibility remain pending review.

## Tradeoffs and alternatives

Support detail improves feasibility but can turn a short activity into an administrative exercise. Reveal details when the chosen next move depends on them; leave unresolved questions visible in the final plan. Authored choices reduce writing burden but constrain expression. Permit replacement wording, disagreement and stopping without rewarding script conformity.

Retain dissent that practice is the wrong intervention. A non-learning route is to clarify the current owner, repair template access, inspect the rota and arrange coverage before offering optional rehearsal. The candidate can expose these options but cannot authorize or verify organizational change.

Provide two plan sheets labelled Initial proposal and Current proposal. Each has spaces for observation, invitation, proposed next move, needed workflow support, authority still needed and unresolved questions. Provide support cards for unknown, unavailable and available in this fictional situation, and a reminder that colleague agreement is unresolved. Facilitation instructions: establish voluntary participation, covered time, suitable space and participant-controlled disposal before starting. Do not solicit personal accounts. Prepare a fictional interaction walkthrough: choose template use, set access unavailable and authority unclear, inspect the conditional proposal, then retain the initial interpretation while leaving the colleague’s account unanswered. Change a relevant support condition during a pending replacement; inspect whether renewed review is required. These checks address implementation behavior, not whether the participant learned.

Prepare a recovery walkthrough: enter fictional optional wording, apply a correction, open another replacement and cancel it, then cover using the keyboard. Inspect concealed content through ordinary accessibility navigation and focus position. Resume and inspect the corrected plan. Cancel clearing once, then confirm clearing from the covered screen; inspect that both situations and all draft states are reset. No results are available.

Inspect responsive readability, focus visibility, control labels, fictional labels and authored-dialogue boundaries. Inspect code and runtime behavior for network requests, storage and telemetry. ## Experience and decisions

Open with a short situation board in a consistent reading order: Observed fictional facts, Possible explanations, Missing context. Do not require dragging cards, recognizing color or hovering. Explanation cards remain visibly tentative; selecting one does not move it into the facts area. Keep the colleague’s unheard account visible throughout.

Offer three concrete openings: an observation with an invitation, a question about the handoff process, and a decision to pause while checking context. Choosing an opening displays exact wording and explicitly authored possible dialogue. Include possibilities in which the colleague explains context, questions the interpretation or asks to discuss it later. These are invented examples, not predicted reactions. The participant can choose another opening, reject the example or continue with the account unresolved. No branch is marked as the correct response.

Reveal the supplied additional fictional context: the rota changed, the template was inaccessible to the colleague and the expected owner was unclear. HCD1 — Human-centered designer origin, extending Workforce R1 in sequence 5 and Systems SE2 in sequence 7: make the situation board usable in a linear reading order, with text labels for facts, explanations and missing context. Human reason: device, vision, motor and reading conditions must not determine who can examine ambiguity. System reason: spatial layout and color alone cannot carry meaning. HCD3 — Human-centered designer origin, extending Workforce R2 in sequence 5 and Systems SE1 in sequence 7: show responsibility and unassigned work beside each support-dependent next move. Challenge to the current model
Sequence 13 usefully models dependencies, participation states and recovery. Add an explicit account of what a learner might notice, decide and revise. Otherwise, completed practice could become the main visible signal despite the evidence limits in sequence 8. Activity completion, learning within practice, workplace adaptation and reciprocal usefulness are distinct claims. No transition between them should occur automatically.

Provisional learning model
Use a fictional situation as the unit of analysis. Record the situation’s ambiguity; the lead’s provisional interpretation; what the colleague can question or correct; candidate decisions; workplace dependencies; and evidence that could distinguish competing explanations. Keep these entries separate from private reflection and do not attach them to named employees.

A candidate practice cycle is: choose a fictional situation and format; identify an assumption; try an approach; receive descriptive feedback against participant-reviewed criteria; decide whether to revise; optionally try again with one changed condition. Prompts and examples may be reduced at the participant’s choice. This cycle is a design hypothesis, not evidence that learning or transfer will occur. Participants may pause, reject feedback or leave a disagreement unresolved.

Illustrative model entry
Situation: a fictional lead believes a missed handoff reflects carelessness. Candidate learning need: distinguish an observation from an interpretation and invite information that could change it. Colleague contribution: explain an unclear handoff expectation or challenge the concern. Context hypotheses: conflicting priorities, inadequate coverage or unclear responsibilities. For a later fictional variation, change the authority boundary or introduce a conflicting account. Explore whether the participant recognizes the changed condition and explains a different choice. Repeating a memorized opening would answer a different question. Neither response establishes workplace readiness.

Feedback and dissent
Candidate feedback concerns are whether interpretations remain open to correction, whether both perspectives are considered and whether a proposed next step addresses the stated situation and constraints. Affected people must review these criteria before use. Do not reward speed, eye contact, confidence, script fidelity or agreement with the facilitator. A respectful conversation may end with unresolved disagreement. Preserve dissent over these criteria and over whether a capability map should exist at all.

Human requirements proposed for review

Provide untimed accessible choices, optional prompts, pause, scenario replacement and editable reflection. It is a rehearsal contribution, not an approved requirement. No participant observations, stakeholder consensus, human authorization or measured learning outcomes exist. Field evidence remains pending.

Learning problem to investigate
The proposed capability map should distinguish knowing a conversation approach, using it in fictional practice, adapting it under workplace constraints and achieving an outcome that both people regard as respectful and useful. These are different claims. Course completion establishes neither readiness nor transfer. A polished rehearsal alone cannot establish workplace effectiveness, and a difficult workplace outcome does not by itself establish a capability deficit.

Discovery should explore three questions through fictional or generalized situations: What does the lead need to notice and decide? What should the colleague be able to question, clarify or change? What conditions make a useful conversation possible? Invite voluntary perspectives from leads, colleagues, managers, learning teams and employee representatives using the accessible choices proposed in sequence 6. Do not solicit recordings or identifiable accounts. Preserve conflicting answers rather than turning them into a common standard prematurely.

Provisional mapping template
For each fictional situation, record: the intended benefit for both people; decisions and adaptations that might require practice; competing workplace explanations; access and coverage conditions; unresolved dissent; and evidence needed to distinguish the hypotheses. Keep entries about situations and supports, not named employees.

Example hypothesis: a lead struggles to open a conversation when the concern is ambiguous. A possible learning need is distinguishing observations from interpretations and inviting correction. Rival explanations include unclear expectations, insufficient time to check the concern or fear of contradicting a manager. A next discovery step is to ask whether a fictional example presents a learning difficulty, a workplace barrier or both. No response or result is assumed.

Candidate learning approach
If discovery supports a learning need, consider short, protected practice sessions with participant-chosen fictional scenarios. Candidate supports include an optional example, prompts that can be reduced as desired, another attempt after feedback and a later variation requiring adaptation. These are design hypotheses to review, not a validated prescription. Participants should be able to pause, choose a written format, reject a scenario and challenge feedback. Agree what feedback concerns before practice; do not equate speed, eye contact, confidence or script fidelity with competence.

Evidence boundaries
A later evidence plan should distinguish participant experience, behavior in fictional practice and voluntary accounts of workplace use. Each answers a different question. Self-reported use may inform improvement but cannot alone establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Consider rival explanations such as changed workload, stronger managerial support, selective participation or familiarity with the practice task. Missing evidence must remain unknown, never a deficit. Evidence-sharing choices should be separate from access to learning, with audiences, retention and withdrawal limits established through human review.

Human and system responsibilities
Humans must judge acceptable outcomes, participation conditions, facilitation quality and whether staffing or workflow changes should precede training. Any system should support accessible practice and private reflection while keeping hypotheses, barriers and uncertainty visible. It cannot certify freely chosen participation or determine readiness from activity traces.

Non-AI option and next action
Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional scenarios, accessible written alternatives and private reflection. This option also needs covered time and human review. Next, incorporate the distinctions above into the provisional discovery protocol and mapping template, then seek affected-person review before field discovery. Preserve dissent over whether a map is needed at all. Modeling should await an explicit account of which needs remain hypotheses and what evidence is still absent.","content_hash":"a18c14b64bc7e98504dcbe6dcc0ed7a8b80810d6642462d7916b013813f91191","revision":1}},"status":"preserved_parent_context"},"prev_hash":"7f8b5394161deec7512d1feca377f4aacc5f387bab69225a381cf4a2a6eb8504","seq":2,"stage":"understand"}

response.artifact_body:
## Problem and people

Conversation Lab proposes fictional practice for first-time team leads. The supplied facts are that a handoff note was absent on Monday, the next shift repeated a check, and the lead has not heard the colleague’s account. The intended learning task is to distinguish observation from explanation, invite missing information and choose a feasible next move. The note’s absence does not establish carelessness, responsibility or why the check was repeated.

New leads, colleagues, managers, learning teams and employee representatives are prospective affected groups. None participate in this demonstration. This is a Learning scientist expert draft for Design, not an approved requirement or demonstrated expertise.

Sequence 2 preserves parent framing, Map and Design as background. Its parent Design addresses a hypothetical staffing interruption on a shared workstation; that event was not observed. Sequences 5, 7 and 9 develop workflow dependencies, correction, recovery, dissent and accessible choices. These are supplied design contributions, not evidence that the activity works.

The learning challenge is that choosing an authored opening and assembling a polished plan may primarily demonstrate use of the offered support. Completion, accepting feedback, changing wording and performing another supported situation cannot establish competence, retention or transfer.

## Human and system capability

Human requirements: participants need discretion to question feedback, retain an interpretation as tentative, revise one part of a plan, request examples or stop. Facilitators need to distinguish a difficulty with the decision from reading demands, language preferences, unclear instructions or unavailable workflow support. Managers must examine coverage, accessible materials, ownership and authority before treating conversation practice as appropriate. No resources, support owners or participation protections have been secured.

Practitioners and affected people must review the proposed feedback focus: whether wording distinguishes observation from explanation, invites an account and makes the next step conditional on feasible support and agreement. These are proposed criteria, not a settled communication standard. Dissent over their usefulness must remain visible. Speed, confidence, eye contact, preferred phrasing and agreement with a facilitator are not proposed criteria.

System requirements: show the participant’s decision and its consequences in the fictional exercise. Distinguish authored examples from participant wording, fictional disclosures from complete causal explanations, and proposed next moves from agreements. Keep feedback descriptive and contestable. Do not create scores, capability labels, aid-use counts or inferred readiness.

Use fictional inputs only, with no identifiable records, profiling, telemetry, storage or network requests. Session state is volatile. Refresh or closure loses work. Access, suitable space, protected time and facilitation workload remain unknown.

## Experience and decisions

The meaningful first decision is how to open an inquiry: state an observation and invite an account; examine the handoff process; or pause to check missing context. Show exact wording and a clearly labelled authored possible exchange. Choosing an opening changes that preview and the questions still to resolve; it does not produce a predicted human reaction. Include disagreement and postponement possibilities without ranking them.

After the initial proposal, reveal the supplied fictional context: the rota changed, the template was inaccessible to the colleague and the expected owner was unclear. Ask the participant to retain or reconsider the interpretation and next move through choices. Do not require a written explanation. The reveal changes available information and the feasibility of some actions; it does not establish a complete account or mandate a particular phrase.

Display brief descriptive feedback beside the current proposal. For an interpretation such as carelessness, say that the missing note is an observation while its reason remains uncertain. For a template-dependent move, state that access and ownership remain unresolved. For a process question, identify what it seeks to clarify and what it still leaves unanswered. For postponement, show that immediate agreement is deferred and that support or a suitable opportunity remains to be arranged. Feedback should describe these implications without praise, blame or correctness labels.

Let the participant reject the feedback, retain the proposal with unresolved conditions, or revise one element: observation, invitation or next move. A focused retry means trying the revised opening against another authored possibility, such as a colleague questioning the interpretation or requesting a later discussion. Label this as another invented possibility, not evidence that revision improves a real conversation. Repetition is optional.

Produce a correctable comparison of Initial proposal and Current proposal, including what was retained, what changed, workflow dependencies and unanswered questions. Do not use revision count or the amount of changed text as progress. A participant who retains wording should receive the same neutral treatment as one who revises it. A retained next move must still display the newly revealed constraints.

Choices and previews must produce a useful plan without text entry. Keep at most two optional open-text fields on the main path: replacement wording and an unresolved question. Display exact proposed changes and their dependency summary before Apply or Cancel. Cancel preserves the current proposal. Follow sequence 7’s requirement for renewed review when relevant conditions change during a pending correction.

Cover/resume must restore the corrected state and offer an optional orientation to the current proposal. Do not require unaided recall before resumption. The interruption concern preserved in sequence 2 changes the recovery requirement: remembering after an interruption cannot become an entry condition or a competence signal. Confirmed clearing remains separate and removes every scenario, draft and pending review, including the optional second situation.

Offer the supplied second situation: two shifts each understood the other to own the final checklist check. Show the situation first with fewer opening suggestions, while allowing the participant to request support immediately. Invite a next move that addresses the disputed ownership rather than carrying forward assumptions about template access. Show which suggestions are available now, but do not record their use. This is another supported practice opportunity, not a transfer test.

## Requirements and rationale

LS1 — Learning scientist origin, extending Workforce R1/R3 in sequence 5, Systems SE2 in sequence 7 and HCD2 in sequence 9: connect each opening and next move to descriptive, contestable feedback. Human reason: participants need to examine a decision rather than infer a preferred answer from praise. System reason: a selected script otherwise conceals the assumption and remaining uncertainty. Interaction: show what the wording states, what account it invites and what dependency remains; allow retaining, rejecting or revising it. Acceptance check: a reviewer can choose each opening, identify its distinct implications and reject the feedback without receiving a correctness label or losing access. The seed supplies the decisions; the feedback criteria remain pending affected-person review.

LS2 — Learning scientist origin, extending the revision cycle preserved in sequence 2 and the correction rules in sequences 7 and 9: provide one optional focused retry after changed fictional context. Human reason: deliberate practice needs a decision that can be reconsidered, rather than compulsory repetition or six reflection boxes. System reason: a before/after display alone can make revision look like the outcome. Interaction: retain the initial proposal, reveal context, permit changing one component, review the exact replacement and optionally preview another authored response. Acceptance check: retaining, revising, cancelling and stopping all leave an accurate current plan; inaccessible template use remains conditional regardless of the chosen wording. No learning effect is established by this check.

LS3 — Learning scientist origin, extending the learning distinctions preserved in sequence 2 and the optional second situation in sequences 5, 7 and 9: separate supported performance, delayed retention and adaptation to changed conditions. Human reason: another prompted attempt does not establish later independent capability. System reason: reduced suggestions can become an implicit test or ranking. Interaction: label the second situation as supported practice, keep suggestions available on request and preserve new ownership uncertainty in its output. Acceptance check: the second situation does not inherit the first situation’s inaccessible-template fact, does not label fewer prompts as greater competence and does not describe completion as transfer. Later retention and workplace adaptation remain unknown.

LS4 — Learning scientist origin, responding to the hypothetical interruption preserved in sequence 2 and extending Systems SE3 and HCD4 in sequences 7 and 9: recovery must not test memory. Human reason: a participant recalled to cover work needs an understandable return, not another demand. System reason: restored historical or rejected wording could distort both the task and its interpretation. Interaction: offer optional orientation after explicit Resume and restore current corrections and unresolved support. Acceptance check: a reviewer can resume and continue without recalling the opening; cancelled wording does not reappear as current; clearing from Cover removes both situations. No interruption, technical check or recovery outcome has been observed.

## Tradeoffs and alternatives

Examples reduce entry burden but may encourage imitation. Keep their status visible, allow rejection and offer fewer initial suggestions in the optional second situation. Removing all support would introduce access and workload demands; support withdrawal is not a success criterion.

Feedback can make decisions inspectable but may privilege the designers’ assumptions. Preserve dissent that the proposed criteria or activity are inappropriate. Organizational repair is a legitimate alternative: inspect the rota, clarify ownership, restore template access and arrange coverage before deciding whether voluntary practice adds value. The tool cannot authorize those changes.

Complete non-AI activity materials: provide a situation card with the three supplied facts; a board labelled Observed facts, Possible explanations and Missing context; and three opening cards containing the observation-and-invitation, process-inquiry and pause wording proposed in sequence 5. Include blank replacement, Pass and Stop cards. Provide a reveal card stating the changed rota, inaccessible template and unclear expected owner, labelled as invented context rather than a complete explanation.

Provide response cards reading “I question that interpretation”, “Here is additional context” and “I would prefer to discuss this later”. These are authored possibilities, not predictions. Provide Initial proposal and Current proposal sheets with spaces for observation, invitation, next move, support, authority, unassigned work and unresolved questions. Provide support cards labelled Unknown, Unavailable and Available in this fictional situation, plus a reminder that colleague agreement remains unresolved.

Provide a feedback card with three prompts: “Which wording states an observation or an explanation?”, “Whose account or agreement is still missing?” and “What support makes the proposed move feasible?” Add a blank cover sheet and the second-situation card: “Two shifts each understood the other to own the final checklist check.” Do not initially supply opening cards for that variation, but make them available on request.

Facilitation: first arrange voluntary participation, protected time, suitable space, accessible materials and participant-controlled disposal. Present the first situation and invite an opening or Pass. Release the reveal, then use the feedback card to describe the proposal without grading it. Invite retaining or changing one component. Offer an optional retry using a response card, the second situation, or stopping. Written selection is sufficient; speech and role-play are optional. Do not solicit personal accounts, collect sheets, photograph work, grade aid use or require sharing. Use the cover sheet for interruption and resume only by participant choice. Dispose of materials under the arrangement agreed before starting. These conditions remain unsecured.

## Acceptance checks

Proposed feedback walkthrough: choose an opening, inspect its specific implications, reveal context and retain the initial interpretation as tentative. Reject a suggested phrase and finish with an unresolved support request. Inspect that descriptive feedback remains available and no completion, conformity or capability judgment appears.

Proposed revision walkthrough: change only the next move, review its exact wording, cancel, retry and apply. Cover and resume without a recall task. Inspect that history, current wording, pending changes and unresolved dependencies remain distinct. No technical behavior has been observed.

Proposed second-situation walkthrough: enter the two-shift ownership situation, request suggestions and construct a proposal without mandatory writing. Inspect that only supplied facts carry forward, help remains available and no transfer claim appears. Practitioner and affected-person review must separately examine comprehension, relevance, dignity, access and workload. Passing interaction checks would establish only the behavior inspected.

## Evidence and unknowns

Actual earlier references are sequence 2, the preserved-parent verification event; sequence 5, the Workforce draft; sequence 7, the Systems engineer draft; and sequence 9, the Human-centered designer draft. The interruption within sequence 2 is hypothetical. The seed supplies fictional source material. No participant observation, consensus, approval, technical result, field pilot or empirical success exists. Field evidence remains pending.

This contribution adds choice-specific feedback, an optional focused retry and explicit separation of second-situation practice from retention and transfer. It retains the recovery change made after the hypothetical interruption. These refine current Design; no supplied event invalidates the earlier Map.

Immediate supported performance, delayed retention and workplace adaptation require different evidence. The candidate produces a reviewable proposal only. A later voluntary revisit of fictional material could explore retention under stated support conditions; it is outside this candidate’s evidence and cannot use stored participant traces. Workplace adaptation would require separately reviewed, voluntary inquiry into changed circumstances and reciprocal usefulness. Neither is authorized or demonstrated here.

Unknowns include whether these decisions reflect a meaningful learning need, whether feedback is understood, whether the second situation demands meaningful adaptation and whether protected time is feasible. Rival explanations for apparent improvement include familiarity, copied examples, facilitator cues, selective participation, repaired workflow and stronger managerial support. Fluent wording may coexist with unresolved understanding; hesitation may reflect access demands rather than a capability deficit.

## Next decision

Carry these proposed learning interactions into the Design synthesis and a subsequent candidate Build. Prepare fictional walkthroughs and seek practitioner and affected-person review of the task, feedback criteria, support and credible refusal before field use. Keep intended quality, future observed technical behavior and untested learning, retention, transfer and flourishing separate. No approval, launch or efficacy decision is supported.
